reviews.repairItems: Don't chase pinholes. reviews.repairItems: Fit a high-efficiency aluminum radiator sized for the big block. Note the experienced-builder tip: an oversize 2-row aluminum core with large (1.0-1.25 inch) tubes generally out-cools a cheap 3- or 4-row aluminum unit, because too many rows restrict airflow. Add a proper full fan shroud (critical — it forces air through the whole core) and either a correct clutch fan or a high-CFM electric fan/dual-fan setup with a thermostatic switch for idle and traffic. Round it out with a correct thermostat, a 7-lb-plus cap, and back-flushed or new heater/cooling plumbing. Done right the big block stays cool in traffic and on the strip.

reviews.repairItems: Pull the cowl vent grille and inspect/clean the plenum; if the inner cowl is perforated, weld in a reproduction cowl vent panel and cowl side panels rather than sealing over rust. Re-open and keep the cowl drains clear, fully seam-seal the rebuilt cowl and the A-pillar/rain-gutter seams, and fit a correct hood-to-cowl seal. reviews.repairItems: Verify true consumption with a documented oil-consumption test (dealers accept roughly 1 qt/2,000 mi as 'normal' but will investigate worse). Cheap first steps: install a catch can / air-oil separator to stop oil ingestion and check/replace the PCV components. Persistent high consumption points to valve seals or worn rings and may require top-end work or, in severe cases, a short-block/engine replacement, sometimes covered under powertrain warranty if documented early. Use the correct spec oil (5W-30 for LS3/LT1) and monitor level frequently between changes.

reviews.repairItems: Convert to electronic ignition. The clean-but-stock-looking route is a Pertronix Ignitor module inside the original distributor (keeps the period look, no firewall clearance issues). For more spark, fit a small-body HEI distributor — the small cap clears the firewall on '67-'69 cars where the big-cap GM HEI does not — and run a dedicated full-12-volt feed from the fuse box, bypassing the factory resistance wire, since electronic ignition needs the full voltage. Before converting an old distributor, do the 'wiggle test' on the shaft; if the bushings are worn, rebuild or replace the distributor first. Result: set-and-forget ignition, stronger spark and easy starting.

If valve body wear or shift solenoid issues are found, install a valve body repair kit or replace the affected solenoids during overhaul. reviews.repairItems: Confirm low fuel pressure before replacing parts by testing pressure at the TBI or CPI rail and checking pump current draw, fuel pump relay operation, wiring at the tank connector, and frame ground integrity. reviews.repairItems: Confirm no misfire or fuel-trim codes are present first (fix those before the cat, or a new converter will fail again). Compare Bank 2 upstream vs downstream O2 sensor data on a scan tool — a downstream sensor that switches rapidly with the upstream one indicates a worn converter; a flat/lazy downstream sensor points to the sensor itself. Replace the Bank 2 downstream O2 sensor first when readings are ambiguous (cheaper), and replace the rear catalytic converter if the substrate is confirmed spent. Inspect the rear exhaust manifold and gaskets for leaks, which can also trip P0430.

reviews.repairItems: Start with the cheapest, most likely fix: inspect the gas-cap O-ring for cracking/dry-rot and re-tighten until it clicks several times; replace with an OEM ACDelco cap if the seal is degraded. Replace the purge or vent solenoid only if the smoke test localizes the leak there; if the underbody EVAP line is rusted, replace the line rather than throwing solenoids at it. Clear the code and complete a drive cycle to confirm.

reviews.repairItems: For early-stage issues (harsh shifts, slipping), a fluid change with ACDelco DEXRON VI and a pressure control solenoid replacement ($200-$400) may resolve the problem. reviews.repairItems: Pressure-test the cooling system and inspect around the lower intake manifold for external seepage; if coolant is disappearing or the oil is contaminated, remove the upper and lower intake manifold and confirm gasket failure. Repair is to replace the lower intake manifold gaskets with the updated metal/rubber design, install revised intake bolts if specified, change the engine oil and filter, thoroughly flush the Dex-Cool-contaminated cooling system, and refill/bleed with the correct coolant mix while checking for bearing damage if coolant entered the crankcase. reviews.repairItems: Monitor oil level at every fuel stop and top off as needed with 0W-20 or 5W-30 synthetic oil. GM considers up to 1 quart per 2,000 miles "acceptable," but an oil consumption test at the dealer can document excessive use for warranty claims. For out-of-warranty vehicles, switching to a slightly heavier 5W-30 oil can reduce consumption. Severe cases require piston ring replacement ($2,000-$3,500). An Italian tune-up (sustained highway driving at higher RPM) can temporarily help by burning carbon off the rings.

reviews.repairItems: Pressure-test the cooling system and inspect the intake manifold-to-head sealing area for external coolant seepage; if coolant contamination is suspected, check the engine oil for a milky appearance and verify with a combustion leak/cooling system test. The proper repair is to remove the upper components and intake manifold, clean the sealing surfaces thoroughly, and install the updated GM/revised metal-core intake manifold gasket set with new seals, then refill with fresh coolant and change the engine oil and filter if any coolant entered the crankcase. On the 4.3L Vortec, it is also wise to inspect the distributor, CPI/CSFI lines, and manifold bolts during reassembly and torque bolts in the correct sequence to spec. Typical repair cost is about $700-$1,400 at a shop depending on labor rates and whether oil service, coolant flush, or related parts are needed.

reviews.repairItems: Confirm the failure by checking fuel pressure at the rail with a gauge; the 4.3L CPI/CSFI systems are very sensitive to low pressure, and a weak pump will often show hard hot restarts, low pressure under load, or a no-start with little or no prime. Inspect the fuel pump electrical connector and ground at the frame, then replace the in-tank pump module with a quality complete assembly that includes the strainer and fuel level sender rather than installing the pump motor alone; on these trucks it is common to drop the tank, though lifting the bed is often faster and reduces rusted strap bolt issues. Replace the fuel filter at the same time and inspect the harness pigtail for heat damage, then verify pressure and gauge operation after repair. Typical repair cost is about $450-$900 parts and labor depending on whether a full module, sender, and connector are needed.

reviews.repairItems: Raise the front suspension and check the lower ball joints for vertical and lateral play with a pry bar and dial indicator, following GM service specs; also inspect the control arm, tire wear pattern, and front-end alignment because worn joints often damage related components. If any looseness or torn boots are found, replace both lower ball joints on the axle as a pair using quality greasable joints or complete control arms where applicable, then torque all fasteners to spec and perform a full front-end alignment. On 4WD S-10 models, inspect the upper joints, idler arm, and tie-rod ends at the same time since wear commonly occurs together. Typical repair cost is about $300-$700 for both lower ball joints with alignment, but can exceed $900 if control arms or additional steering parts are needed.

reviews.repairItems: Diagnose with a running-compression test on the misfiring cylinder (an AFM lifter that stays below ~25 PSI regardless of solenoid command is collapsed). Use only the correct oil and keep oil changes on schedule, as low/dirty oil accelerates failure.

reviews.repairItems: GM's progression of TSBs added an AFM oil-deflector/shield and revised PCV provisions and ultimately upgraded the piston rings under warranty. Verified fix is replacement of the pistons/rings (and AFM oil-pressure relief valve / valley-cover shield); many owners opt for an AFM delete with a non-AFM cam, lifters, and tune to permanently resolve it. Settlement payments (~$3,380) were available to eligible owners in CA, ID, and NC who had not already received free warranty piston repairs.

reviews.repairItems: Under NHTSA recall 25V274 / GM N252494000, dealers inspect the engine. Failed or out-of-spec engines receive a full long-block replacement; engines that pass inspection get an oil-and-filter change switching from 0W-20 to the heavier 0W-40, a new oil-fill cap, and an owner's-manual insert. Owners hearing knocking, seeing low oil pressure, or noticing metallic debris should stop driving and contact a dealer. reviews.repairItems: Do NOT replace parts off the P0700 alone. Use a bidirectional/TCM-capable scan tool to read the companion codes stored in the transmission controller and verify transmission fluid level and condition first (low or burnt DEXRON-VI fluid alone can trigger the chain). For 6L80 trucks, a failed internal TEHCM is confirmed by multiple simultaneous solenoid/pressure codes; the fix is to drop the pan and replace the TEHCM, which MUST then be programmed to the vehicle's VIN with GM calibration files before the truck will start or shift correctly (ordering the OEM unit by the last 8 VIN digits can yield a plug-and-play unit needing no fast-adapt relearn). For 4L60E trucks, replace the specific failed shift solenoid or internal mode switch identified by the sub-code. Repair the wiring/connectors to the TCM if corrosion is found. On very new 2023-2025 Silverado 1500s, P0700 paired with P0747 is a known valve-body defect covered by Safety Recall N242454440 / Special Coverage N242454441 — check the VIN with a dealer for a free repair.

However, the stabilizer often masks worn front-end components — inspect all ball joints, tie rod ends, wheel bearings, and track bar bushings. Replace any worn components found. A comprehensive front-end alignment ($100-$150) should follow any steering component replacement. For lifted trucks, an upgraded dual steering stabilizer kit ($150-$300) provides better oscillation damping. Proper tire balance is critical — even slight imbalance can trigger the wobble.

reviews.repairItems: Replace idler arm, pitman arm, inner and outer tie rods, and center link as a set. Get alignment after. Consider Cognito steering brace kit for prevention.

reviews.repairItems: On a misfire/tick, pull the valve covers and inspect the AFM lifters and corresponding cam lobes. Keep oil changes on time and avoid extended intervals — degraded/low oil pressure accelerates AFM lifter failure.

reviews.title: HVAC Blend Door Actuator Failure (Clicking Dash)
reviews.howToFix: Replace the failed actuator (GM 89018365 / AC Delco 15-73989 / Dorman 604-106 for the main blend actuator). After installation, run the HVAC recalibration by pulling the HVAC fuse for ~60 seconds and cycling the key so the module relearns the door stops. Identify which actuator by whether the click tracks with temperature (blend) or airflow direction (mode).

reviews.repairItems: Repair or replace the cluster. The permanent fix is to replace the failed X27.168 stepper motors (sold in 6-motor repair kits with upgraded motors and backlight bulbs) and re-flow the board solder, or install a remanufactured cluster. The cluster is a ~1-hour DIY removal (7mm socket + trim tool); a rebuilt/repaired unit keeps the original odometer mileage. Many owners send the cluster to a rebuild service for $150-250.

reviews.repairItems: Replace the corroded rear A/C lines ($200-$600 for parts). Labor is 2-4 hours ($200-$500) as the lines must be routed under the vehicle. The entire A/C system must be evacuated before repair and recharged afterward ($100-$200 for evacuation and recharge). Also replace the receiver/drier ($30-$60) whenever the system has been open to the atmosphere. Some shops fabricate replacement lines from copper tubing and compression fittings, which resists corrosion better than the OEM steel lines. Apply undercoating or wax coating to new lines to prevent future corrosion.

reviews.repairItems: The steering column lock actuator module needs replacement ($150-$400 for parts, $200-$400 labor). reviews.repairItems: Replace the leaking seal(s) — the rear output shaft seal is $10-$20 for the part and 1-2 hours of labor ($100-$250). The front output seal is similar but harder to access. If the case halves are leaking, resealing requires splitting the case ($400-$800 labor). Check the transfer case fluid level every oil change and change the fluid every 50,000 miles with the GM-specified Auto-Trak II (NP246) or DEXRON VI (NP261/NP263). Low fluid is a transfer case killer — check before it is too late.

reviews.repairItems: Verify fluid level and color first (burnt/dark red = internal wear). Scan for solenoid/pressure codes. reviews.repairItems: Follow recall 25V-274: dealer inspects the engine and replaces it if it fails inspection; vehicles that pass receive higher-viscosity 0W-40 dexos oil, a new oil filter, and an updated oil-fill cap specifying the new viscosity. Owners hearing a knock, seeing low oil pressure, or getting loss-of-propulsion warnings should stop driving and contact a dealer. Out-of-warranty engine replacement absent recall coverage runs well into five figures — verify VIN eligibility with GM before paying.

reviews.repairItems: Pressure-test the cooling system and inspect the throttle body heater hoses/port, thermostat housing, and the water pump weep hole on the 4.2L Atlas I6; dried coolant residue below the pump pulley or around the throttle body usually confirms the source. Replace any leaking throttle body heater hose or fitting, the thermostat housing and seal if seepage is present, and the water pump if coolant is coming from the weep hole; on these engines it is also wise to install a new thermostat and fresh Dex-Cool coolant during service. After repair, vacuum-fill or properly bleed the system and verify fan clutch operation and operating temperature on a road test. Typical repair cost ranges from about $150-$300 for hoses or housing repairs, and roughly $500-$900 for a water pump replacement depending on labor rates and parts quality.

reviews.repairItems: Confirm fan clutch operation with a scan tool by comparing commanded fan speed to actual speed and checking for related DTCs such as P1481, P1482, P1484, or P0526, then inspect the fan clutch harness and connector for oil contamination or damaged wiring. If the clutch is stuck engaged, freewheeling, or not responding to PCM commands, replace the electronic viscous fan clutch assembly; on many TrailBlazers this is a bolt-on repair requiring fan shroud removal and a special fan clutch wrench/holding tool. After replacement, clear codes, verify fan engagement during warm idle and A/C operation, and confirm coolant temperature stays stable in traffic. Typical repair cost is about $300-$700 total depending on brand of clutch and labor time, with OEM-quality parts strongly recommended.

reviews.repairItems: Confirm the failure by checking static and running refrigerant pressures, verifying compressor clutch command/power and ground, and inspecting for noise, seizure, or metal contamination in the oil and lines. If the compressor has failed internally, replace the compressor, receiver/drier or condenser assembly (the drier is integrated on many GM systems), expansion valve/orifice components as applicable, thoroughly flush any reusable lines and evaporator, evacuate the system, and recharge with the exact specified refrigerant and PAG oil; also inspect cooling fan operation and high-side pressures so an overpressure condition does not destroy the replacement unit. If debris is present, a simple compressor swap often leads to repeat failure, so a full system cleanout is the correct repair. Typical cost is about $1,200-$2,500 for a complete repair depending on how many contaminated components must be replaced.

reviews.repairItems: Check for and install any available OTA software updates through the Settings menu. Perform a hard reset by holding the power/volume knob for 10+ seconds. In rare cases, the infotainment module hardware must be replaced.
